description.summary: Implement a standalone counter with increment, decrement, and reset. Guard the decrement at zero, disable the minus button when the value is 0, and keep the count in one signal so every binding that shows it updates with it.

requirements: Use a standalone Angular component as the root component.
Display the current count value.
Provide "+", "-", and "Reset" buttons.
Disable the decrement button when the count is 0.
expectedBehavior: Clicking "+" increases the count by 1.
Clicking "-" decreases the count by 1, but never below 0.
Clicking "Reset" sets the count back to 0.
implementationNotes: Hold the count in a signal (`count = signal(0)`) and change it with `update` or `set`; the template reads it as `count()`. A plain `count = 0` field also works here, because every change comes from a click in this template.
Use template event bindings like `(click)="..."` for button actions.
Derive the disabled state with `computed` instead of repeating `count() === 0` in the template. No child components are needed.

solutionBlock.overview:
The counter needs one piece of state, the current count. The solution keeps it in a signal, `count = signal(0)`, on the standalone root component and derives `isZero` from it with `computed`. The three buttons call `inc()`, `dec()` and `reset()`, which change the signal with `update` and `set`. The template reads `count()` and binds `[disabled]="isZero()"` on the minus button, so Angular knows which bindings depend on the count and the component can use `OnPush` change detection.

**Test cases**
- Click "+" once → count becomes `1`.
- Click "+" multiple times → count increases by 1 on each click.
- With count at `0`, "-" is disabled and clicking it does nothing.
- From a positive value, clicking "-" decreases the count by 1, but never below `0`.
- From a positive value, clicking "Reset" sets count back to `0` and disables "-" again.

approaches.title: Signal state with a computed disabled flag
approaches.prose:
Keep the whole counter in `AppComponent`.

1. Declare `count = signal(0)`. Reading `count()` in the template ties that binding to the signal.
2. Derive `isZero = computed(() => this.count() === 0)`. It recalculates only when `count` changes, and the template binds it to the minus button's `disabled`.
3. `inc()` calls `count.update((value) => value + 1)` and `reset()` calls `count.set(0)`. `dec()` clamps with `Math.max(0, value - 1)`, so the count cannot drop below zero even if something calls `dec()` while the button is disabled.
4. In the template, the interpolation becomes `{{ count() }}` and the minus button binds `[disabled]="isZero()"`.

`ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush` is safe because every value the template shows comes from a signal. A plain field with an `isZero` getter would also pass here, since every change starts with a click inside this template. The signal version keeps working when the count later changes from a timer, a service or a parent, where a plain field under `OnPush` or zoneless change detection leaves the view stale.

pitfalls: Allowing the count to go below 0 when handling the decrement.
Forgetting to bind the disabled state of the decrement button, which makes the UX unclear.
Writing `{{ count }}` instead of `{{ count() }}`: the template then shows the signal function, not the number.
Changing the count inline in the template (`count.set(count() - 1)`) instead of in methods, which spreads the zero guard across bindings.
techniques: Standalone components are the default since Angular 19, so the decorator needs neither `standalone: true` nor `CommonModule`.
Holding state in a `signal` and changing it with `set` and `update`.
Deriving view state with `computed` instead of a getter.
Using `OnPush` change detection, which signal-driven templates keep correct.

description.summary: Build a contact form using an Angular standalone component and reactive forms. You will work in `src/app/app.component.ts` and register `provideHttpClient()` in `src/main.ts` – the HTML and CSS are already set up. On submit, validate the input and send the form data with a POST request to a fake JSON API endpoint, showing loading, success, and error states.

requirements: Put the form and request logic in the standalone root component in `src/app/app.component.ts` (template and styles are already provided), and register `HttpClient` with `provideHttpClient()` in `src/main.ts`.
Build/configure a reactive form with fields for name, email, and message.
Make all fields required; validate email with a basic email validator.
Disable the submit button while the form is invalid or while a request is in progress.
On valid submit, send a POST request with the form body to `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts` using HttpClient.
If the request succeeds, set `successMessage` to `"Your message has been sent. Thank you!"`.
If the request fails, set `errorMessage` to `"Something went wrong. Please try again."`.
Track an `isSubmitting` flag so the user cannot trigger multiple requests at the same time.
expectedBehavior: Initially, the submit button is disabled until the form becomes valid (all required fields filled and email valid).
If the user attempts to submit invalid data, all controls are marked as touched and validation error messages are shown for the affected fields.
On a valid submit, a POST request is sent to `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts` and the button is disabled while `isSubmitting` is true.
On success, `isSubmitting` becomes false, `successMessage` is set to `"Your message has been sent. Thank you!"`, and the form may optionally be reset.
On error, `isSubmitting` becomes false, `errorMessage` is set to `"Something went wrong. Please try again."`, and the user can fix the issue and resubmit.
implementationNotes: Configure the reactive form and all request/UX logic inside `AppComponent` in `app.component.ts`. The CSS stays as it is; the HTML changes only if you keep the request state in signals, where its bindings become calls (`isSubmitting()`, `successMessage()`, `errorMessage()`).
Use `ReactiveFormsModule` and `FormBuilder` to define the form group for the contact form.
Use Angular's built-in validators such as `Validators.required` and `Validators.email` (and optionally `Validators.minLength` for the message).

Inject `HttpClient` with `inject(HttpClient)` and register it once with `provideHttpClient()` in the `bootstrapApplication` providers in `src/main.ts`. A component's `providers` array cannot take it (Angular throws NG0207 for environment providers there), and `HttpClientModule` is deprecated.

Keep `isSubmitting`, `successMessage` and `errorMessage` in signals. The `subscribe` callbacks run after `submit()` has returned, and a signal write is what refreshes an `OnPush` view from there; plain fields need the default change detection strategy and zone.js.
Clear previous `successMessage` / `errorMessage` at the start of `submit()` so only the latest result is shown.
Call `markAllAsTouched()` on the form before checking validity, so error messages appear when the user submits incomplete data.
Use `isSubmitting` both in the button's `[disabled]` binding and as an early return in `submit()`: `(ngSubmit)` still calls `submit()` while the button is disabled.
On success, you can reset the form to its initial state while keeping the success message visible.
techFocus: Standalone component setup with reactive forms
Form validation and UX (disabled submit, inline errors, touched state)
`HttpClient` registered with `provideHttpClient()`, a fake POST endpoint and request lifecycle handling
Loading, success, and error state held in signals

solutionBlock.overview:
This exercise combines a standalone component, a reactive form and `HttpClient`. `contactForm` is a `FormGroup` with `name`, `email` and `message` controls built with `FormBuilder`, and the template reads its validity and touched state directly. The request lifecycle lives in three signals, `isSubmitting`, `successMessage` and `errorMessage`, which the template calls as `isSubmitting()`, `successMessage()` and `errorMessage()`. `HttpClient` is registered once with `provideHttpClient()` in `src/main.ts` and injected with `inject(HttpClient)`.

`submit()` clears both messages, marks every control as touched so the inline errors appear, and returns while the form is invalid or a request is still running. Otherwise it sets `isSubmitting` and posts `contactForm.value` to `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts`. On success it shows `"Your message has been sent. Thank you!"` and resets the form, which leaves the button disabled until the fields are valid again. On error it shows `"Something went wrong. Please try again."` and keeps the typed values, so the user can send them again.

**Test cases**
- With all fields empty, the submit button is disabled.
- Typing an invalid email keeps the form invalid and disabled.
- Tapping submit with invalid fields marks controls as touched and shows validation errors.
- With valid inputs, clicking submit triggers a POST request to `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts` and disables the button while `isSubmitting` is `true`.
- On success, `"Your message has been sent. Thank you!"` is shown and the form can optionally reset.
- On error, `"Something went wrong. Please try again."` is shown and the user can resubmit.

approaches.title: Reactive form with the request state in signals
approaches.prose:
Build `contactForm` with `inject(FormBuilder)`: `name` is required, `email` uses `Validators.required` and `Validators.email`, and `message` uses `Validators.required` and `Validators.minLength(10)`. `f = this.contactForm.controls` gives the template short paths for its error checks, such as `f.email.errors?.['email']`; the controls object never changes, so `f` is a plain field, not a getter.

The request state is three signals: `isSubmitting = signal(false)`, `successMessage = signal('')` and `errorMessage = signal('')`, and the button binds `[disabled]="contactForm.invalid || isSubmitting()"`. `submit()` runs from both `(ngSubmit)` and the button's `(click)`. It clears the messages, calls `markAllAsTouched()`, and returns when the form is invalid or `isSubmitting()` is already true, so a second submit during a request sends nothing. Otherwise it sets `isSubmitting` and posts `contactForm.value`; `next` clears the flag, sets the success message and resets the form, and `error` clears the flag and sets the error message.

Those callbacks run after `submit()` has returned. Under `OnPush`, plain fields assigned in `error` would leave the button on "Sending…", because nothing there marks the view for check; a signal write does. The form state can stay in the `FormGroup`: typing, blur and submit are template events, which mark the view, and `reset()` runs next to the signal writes in `next`. `HttpClient` comes from `provideHttpClient()` in `bootstrapApplication` in `src/main.ts`. It cannot go in the component's `providers`, because it returns environment providers, and it replaces the deprecated `HttpClientModule`.

pitfalls: Relying on the disabled button alone: `(ngSubmit)` still calls `submit()`, so the method has to return while `isSubmitting()` is true, or a second POST goes out.
Not calling `markAllAsTouched()` before checking validity, so an untouched form fails without showing any inline error.
Assigning plain fields in the `subscribe` callbacks of an `OnPush` component: after a failed request the view stays on "Sending…", because nothing marks it for check.
Adding `provideHttpClient()` to the component's `providers`: it returns environment providers, and Angular throws NG0207. Register it in `bootstrapApplication` in `src/main.ts`.
Hard-coding different success or error messages than the ones specified in the exercise, which may cause tests to fail.
techniques: Building the form with `inject(FormBuilder)` and the built-in `Validators.required`, `Validators.email` and `Validators.minLength`.
Holding loading, success and error state in signals that the `subscribe` callbacks write.
Registering `HttpClient` with `provideHttpClient()` in `bootstrapApplication` and injecting it with `inject(HttpClient)`.
Driving the button's `disabled` state from `contactForm.invalid || isSubmitting()` and repeating the `isSubmitting()` check in `submit()`.
Using a fake HTTP endpoint (`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts`) to simulate a real backend without extra setup.

description.summary: Build a small todo list using an Angular standalone component. Add tasks, mark them complete, remove them, and render stable list identity with modern `@for (...; track ...)` control flow.

requirements: Use a standalone Angular component as the root component.
Display a text input and an "Add" button for creating new todos.
Render todo items with `@for` and `track todo.id`, so each row keeps its identity.
Each todo item should show a label and a checkbox to toggle completion.
Allow removing a single todo item from the list.
Optionally provide a "Clear completed" action to remove all completed todos.
expectedBehavior: Typing a non-empty value and clicking "Add" appends a new todo to the list and clears the input.
Empty or whitespace-only values are ignored (no item is added).
Clicking a todo’s checkbox toggles its completed state.
Completed todos are visually distinguished (e.g. line-through).
Clicking a remove button deletes that specific todo.
If you implement "Clear completed", it removes only the completed todos.
implementationNotes: Keep everything in `AppComponent` (`src/app/app.component.ts` and `app.component.html`). No extra services or components are required.
Store the todos as an array of `{ id, text, done }` objects. Holding the array in a signal and replacing it on every change (`todos.update(...)`) keeps anything computed from it correct.
Use `@for` with `track todo.id` so item identity stays stable without a separate tracking function.
Use `[(ngModel)]` for the input binding (remember to import `FormsModule`); it binds to a signal as well as to a plain field.
Use click handlers like `(click)="addTask()"` and `(click)="removeTask(todo)"` to change the list.
techFocus: Signal state for the input text and the todo list
Rendering lists with `@for` and an explicit `track` expression
Using `[(ngModel)]` for simple form input binding
Basic UX for add / toggle / remove actions

solutionBlock.overview:
This exercise models a classic todo list in a single standalone component. The input text lives in a `newTask` signal bound with `[(ngModel)]`, and the list lives in a `todos` signal holding `{ id, text, done }` objects. `hasTodos` is computed from the list and switches between the list and the empty state. The template renders `@for (todo of todos(); track todo.id)`, and every handler replaces the array through `todos.update(...)` instead of editing it in place.

Typical flow:
- User types into the input; `[(ngModel)]="newTask"` writes each change into the signal.
- Clicking **Add** calls `addTask()`, which trims the text, ignores empties, appends a todo with the next id, and clears `newTask`.
- Each row's checkbox shows `todo.done` through `[checked]` and calls `toggleTask(todo.id)` on change, which swaps in a copy of that todo with `done` flipped; the label gets the `.done` class.
- Clicking the remove button calls `removeTask(todo.id)`, which filters that item out.
- "Clear completed" calls `clearCompleted()`, which keeps only the todos that are not done.

**Test cases**
- With an empty input, clicking **Add** does nothing.
- Typing "Buy milk" and clicking **Add** shows a single todo row with that text.
- Toggling the checkbox marks the item as completed and applies the completed styling.
- Clicking the remove button deletes that specific row.
- After completing multiple todos, clicking "Clear completed" removes only the completed ones.

approaches.title: Signal state with immutable list updates
approaches.prose:
Keep the input text and the list in signals: `newTask = signal('')` and `todos = signal<Todo[]>([])`. A plain `nextId` counter supplies ids; the template never reads it, so it does not need to be a signal. `hasTodos = computed(() => this.todos().length > 0)` drives the `@if` around the list and the footer.

`addTask()` reads `newTask()`, trims it, returns early when it is empty, then appends with `todos.update((todos) => [...todos, { id: this.nextId++, text, done: false }])` and resets the input with `newTask.set('')`. `toggleTask(id)` maps over the list and replaces only the matching todo with `{ ...todo, done: !todo.done }`; `removeTask(id)` and `clearCompleted()` filter.

Every change produces a new array, and a toggled todo is a new object. That is what lets `computed` values and `OnPush` change detection see the change: a signal compares values with `Object.is`, so pushing into the same array or flipping `todo.done` in place leaves the signal unchanged. For the same reason the checkbox uses `[checked]="todo.done"` with `(change)="toggleTask(todo.id)"` instead of `[(ngModel)]="todo.done"`, which writes into the object directly. The text input keeps `[(ngModel)]`, which binds two-way to a signal.

pitfalls: Allowing empty or whitespace-only todos to be added.
Pushing into the array held by the signal or flipping `todo.done` in place: the signal keeps the same reference, so computed values and `OnPush` views miss the change.
Reusing one id for several items, which breaks the identity `track todo.id` relies on.
Forgetting to import `FormsModule`, which breaks `[(ngModel)]` bindings.
techniques: Holding list state in a `signal` and replacing it with `update` on every change.
Deriving `hasTodos` with `computed`.
Binding `[(ngModel)]` two-way to a signal for the text input.
Rendering lists with `@for` and `track todo.id` for stable identity.

description.summary: Build an image slider with next/prev controls, a current index, and disabled states at bounds. Keep the template state-driven, render indicators with modern @for control flow, and update the active slide label as the index changes.

requirements: Use a standalone Angular component as the root component.
Keep an in-memory list of slides (each with at least a title and image URL).
Display the currently active slide (image and title).
Provide "Previous" and "Next" buttons to move between slides.
Disable the "Previous" button on the first slide and the "Next" button on the last slide.
Render dot indicators for each slide; clicking a dot should jump to that slide.
Display a small "Slide X of N" helper text.
expectedBehavior: Initial view shows the first slide.
Clicking "Next" advances to the next slide until the last one; afterwards it stays on the last slide and "Next" becomes disabled.
Clicking "Previous" moves backwards until the first slide; on the first slide it stays there and "Previous" is disabled.
Clicking a dot activates the corresponding slide, updates the main image and title, and updates the "Slide X of N" text.
The active slide's dot is visually highlighted.
implementationNotes: Store slides in a readonly array on the component (e.g. `slides = [...]`).
Track the active slide with a numeric index. Holding it in a signal (`currentIndex = signal(0)`) lets every binding and derived value that reads it update together.
Derive the current slide (`currentSlide`) and the flags `canGoPrev` / `canGoNext` from the index; with a signal index they are `computed` values.
Use template bindings (`(click)`, `[disabled]`, `@for`, `[class.active]`) to wire up the controls and indicators.
No need for routing, services, or external state management; keep everything in the root component.
techFocus: Signal state with derived `computed` values (current slide, canGoPrev/canGoNext)
Template control flow with @for and event bindings
Basic UI state and styling for active and disabled controls

solutionBlock.overview:
The only state that changes in this slider is the position. The solution keeps the slides in a plain `readonly` array, holds the position in `currentIndex = signal(0)`, and derives `currentSlide`, `canGoPrev` and `canGoNext` from it with `computed`. Previous and Next call `prev()` and `next()`, each dot calls `goTo(i)`, and all three methods write `currentIndex`, so the figure, the "Slide X of N" text, the button states and the active dot follow that one value.

**Test cases**
- Initial render shows the first slide, with "Previous" disabled and the first dot highlighted.
- Clicking "Next" repeatedly walks through the slides and disables itself on the last slide.
- Clicking "Previous" from the middle moves backward one slide at a time.
- Clicking a dot jumps directly to that slide and updates the heading, image, and helper text.
- The slider never goes out of range (no index smaller than 0 or greater than `slides.length - 1`).

approaches.title: Index signal with a computed slide and edge flags
approaches.prose:
Keep the slider in `AppComponent`.

1. `slides` is a plain `readonly` array and `totalSlides` is its length. The list never changes, so neither needs a signal.
2. Hold the position in `currentIndex = signal(0)`. It is the only state that changes.
3. Derive `currentSlide = computed(() => this.slides[this.currentIndex()] ?? null)`, and `canGoPrev` and `canGoNext` by comparing `currentIndex()` with `0` and `totalSlides - 1`. A `computed` caches its value until `currentIndex` changes, while a getter runs again every time Angular checks the template.
4. `goTo(index)` returns early for an index outside `0` to `totalSlides - 1`, then calls `currentIndex.set(index)`. `prev()` and `next()` check `canGoPrev()` or `canGoNext()` before `currentIndex.update(...)`, so the index stays in range even if one of them runs while its button is disabled.
5. The template renders the figure inside `@if (currentSlide(); as slide)`, prints `currentIndex() + 1` and `totalSlides` in the helper text, binds `[disabled]="!canGoPrev()"` and `[disabled]="!canGoNext()"`, and marks the active dot with `[class.active]="i === currentIndex()"`.

Every value the template shows comes from `currentIndex` or the fixed list, which is why the component can use `OnPush`. With the starter's plain `currentIndex` field, clicks would still work, because an event in the template marks the view for checking. An autoplay timer that advanced that field would not: under `OnPush` the view would stay on the old slide. Calling `next()` from a timer updates the view here, because it writes the signal.

pitfalls: Letting `currentIndex` leave the range `0` to `slides.length - 1`: `currentSlide()` becomes `null`, the figure disappears and the helper text names a slide that does not exist.
Repeating `slides[currentIndex()]` in several bindings instead of reading the `currentSlide` computed once through the `@if` alias.
Leaving Previous and Next enabled at the ends, so a click on them does nothing visible.
Writing `i === currentIndex` without the call: it compares a number with the signal function, so no dot is ever active.
techniques: Holding the position in a `signal` and changing it with `set` and `update`.
Deriving `currentSlide`, `canGoPrev` and `canGoNext` with `computed` instead of getters.
Unwrapping a nullable computed with `@if (currentSlide(); as slide)`.
Reflecting state with `[class.active]` and `[disabled]`, and tracking the dots with `track slide.id`.

description.summary: Create an accessible Angular tab switcher driven by one typed `activeTab` value. Tab controls update the selection, `@if` renders exactly one panel, and active styles identify the current tab.

requirements: Use a standalone Angular component as the root component.
Render three tabs labeled "Overview", "Details", and "Settings".
Track which tab is currently active and visually highlight it.
Render only the active tab's content at a time.
expectedBehavior: The initial active tab should be "Overview".
Clicking a tab makes it the active tab.
Only the active tab's panel is visible at any time.
The active tab button has a distinct visual style (e.g. underline or background).
implementationNotes: Store the currently active tab in one typed value, such as `activeTab = signal<TabId>('overview')`, and read it through a helper like `isActive(tab)`. A plain typed property also works here, because only clicks in this template change it.
Use event bindings such as `(click)` to switch tabs.
Use modern `@if` control flow to render exactly one panel.
Connect each tab to its panel with tab roles, `aria-selected`, `aria-controls`, and labelled panels.
techFocus: Typed active state in a standalone component
Accessible tab controls and one visible panel

solutionBlock.overview:
This exercise is about modeling a small piece of UI state (which tab is active) and using that state to drive both styles and conditional rendering. A single standalone `AppComponent` holds the selection in `activeTab = signal<TabId>('overview')`, where `TabId` is the union `'overview' | 'details' | 'settings'`. The tab buttons call `selectTab(tab)`, which sets the signal, and `isActive(tab)` reads it for each tab's `[class.active]` and `aria-selected` and for the `@if` around each panel.

**Test cases**
- Initial render shows the Overview panel and its tab appears active.
- Clicking Details switches the active tab and hides Overview content.
- Clicking Settings switches again and only the Settings content is visible.
- Re-clicking an already active tab keeps the same content and styles.

approaches.title: One `activeTab` signal read through `isActive`
approaches.prose:
Keep the whole switcher in `AppComponent`.

1. Define `type TabId = 'overview' | 'details' | 'settings'` and declare `activeTab = signal<TabId>('overview')`. The type argument keeps any other string out of the signal.
2. `isActive(tab)` returns `this.activeTab() === tab`. Because it reads the signal, every binding that calls it depends on `activeTab`: `[class.active]="isActive('overview')"`, `[attr.aria-selected]="isActive('overview')"` and `@if (isActive('overview'))` all change together.
3. `selectTab(tab)` calls `activeTab.set(tab)`. Setting the tab that is already active stores an equal value, so the signal does not notify, the bindings keep their values and the open panel is not recreated.
4. The template follows the ARIA tabs pattern: the nav is the tab list, each button is a `tab` whose `aria-controls` names its panel, and each panel is a `tabpanel` labelled by its tab. Only the active panel exists in the DOM.

The component uses `OnPush`. With a plain `activeTab` field it would still pick up clicks, which mark it for checking, but not a selection set from outside its template, such as a router listener or a timer. With the signal, any `set` call updates the view, whoever makes it.

pitfalls: Hard-coding panel visibility without tying it to a single source of truth for the active tab.
Forgetting to visually differentiate the active tab from inactive ones.
Using separate booleans for each tab instead of a single `activeTab` value, which quickly becomes harder to manage.
Writing `this.activeTab === tab` without the call: it compares the signal function with a string, so it is always false and no panel renders.
techniques: Modeling view state with a union type for clearer intent.
Holding the selection in `signal<TabId>` and changing it with `set`.
Using a helper like `isActive` that reads the signal, so the template stays short and every binding that calls it stays in step.
Applying classes conditionally with `[class.active]` to style the active tab.

description.summary: Filter a user list in Angular by search and role without mutating the original array. Keep the search text, role and active-only toggle in signals, derive the matching users with computed, and show an empty state when no matches exist. Angular focus: derive filtered lists with computed signals.

requirements: Use a standalone Angular component as the root component.
Define a fixed in-memory list of users (name, role, active flag).
Render a search input that filters by name (case-insensitive).
Render a role dropdown (e.g. All, Admin, Editor, Viewer) that filters by role.
Render a checkbox that, when checked, shows only active users.
Render the filtered list below the controls.
expectedBehavior: Initially, all users are shown.
Typing in the search box filters users whose name includes the search text (case-insensitive).
Changing the role dropdown filters by that role (or shows all roles when "All" is selected).
Checking the "Only active" checkbox hides inactive users.
When no users match the filters, an empty state message is shown.
implementationNotes: Keep a static `users` array in the component (no HTTP or services needed).
Hold `searchTerm`, `selectedRole` and `showOnlyActive` in signals. `[(ngModel)]` binds two-way to a writable signal the same way it binds to the starter's plain fields.
Derive `filteredUsers` with `computed` so it applies all three filters and recalculates only when one of them changes; the starter's getter marks where that logic goes.
Use template bindings like `[(ngModel)]` to keep inputs in sync with component state.
For a small list, filtering on the client is fine; with `computed` it reruns when a filter changes, not on every render. You can mention this trade-off in discussion.
techFocus: Derived state with `computed` from a static data source
Template-driven forms (`ngModel`) and list rendering with `@for`

solutionBlock.overview:
This exercise keeps three pieces of UI state, the search text, the selected role and the "only active" toggle, and derives the visible list from them. Each one lives in a signal (`searchTerm`, `selectedRole`, `showOnlyActive`) bound to its control with `[(ngModel)]`. The five entries in `users` never change; `filteredUsers` is a `computed` that applies all three filters on top of that array. The template renders `@for (user of filteredUsers(); track user.id)` and shows the empty row when `filteredUsers().length === 0`.

**Test cases**
- With default state, all users are shown.
- Typing part of a user's name (case-insensitive) narrows the list to matching users.
- Selecting a role shows only users with that role, unless "All" is selected.
- Checking "Only active" hides inactive users.
- Combining search, role filter, and active filter works as expected.
- When filters exclude everything, an empty state row appears.

approaches.title: Filter signals with a computed `filteredUsers`
approaches.prose:
Keep everything in `AppComponent`. Each control writes one signal: `searchTerm = signal('')`, `selectedRole = signal<RoleFilter>('all')` and `showOnlyActive = signal(false)`. `[(ngModel)]="searchTerm"` binds two-way to a writable signal, so the template bindings read the same as with plain fields, and every keystroke, role change or checkbox toggle sets the signal. The `users` array is a constant and stays a plain readonly field.

`filteredUsers` is a `computed` that:
1. Reads the three signals once and normalizes the search term with `trim().toLowerCase()`.
2. Keeps users whose names contain that term, when one is entered.
3. Keeps only users with the selected role, unless the role is `'all'`.
4. Drops inactive users while the toggle is on.

`filter` returns a new array, so `users` itself never changes. The computed reruns only when one of the three signals changes, while a getter would run again every time Angular checks the template. The template calls `filteredUsers()` in the `@for` and in the `@if` that shows the empty row, tracks rows by `user.id` so a row keeps its identity while the filters change, and imports `TitleCasePipe` on its own for the role pill instead of `CommonModule`. All view state is in signals, so the component uses `OnPush`.

pitfalls: Mutating the original `users` array instead of deriving a filtered view.
Forgetting to normalize case when comparing the search term to names.
Applying only one of the filters instead of combining all three.
Filtering in the template or in a getter, which reruns the filter every time Angular checks the component instead of only when a filter changes.
Copying the result into a separate signal from each control's change handler or from an `effect`: it can fall out of step with the filters, while a `computed` cannot.
techniques: Importing `FormsModule` and the standalone `TitleCasePipe` instead of `CommonModule`.
Binding `[(ngModel)]` two-way to writable signals.
Deriving the filtered list with `computed` and keeping the original data unchanged.
Tracking each `@for` row by the user id so identity survives filtering.

description.summary: Build a simple FAQ (accordion) component in Angular using inputs/outputs. Clicking a question should toggle its answer. By default, only one item can be open at a time, but the user can enable a mode where multiple items can stay open. Concepts: components, inputs, outputs. Angular focus: signal inputs and an output for each item, and a parent that holds the open indexes in a signal.

requirements: Use a standalone root component and at least one child component for a single FAQ item.
Render a list of 3–4 FAQ items (question + answer) from an in-memory array.
Clicking on a question toggles its answer open/closed.
In the default mode, only one FAQ item can be open at a time.
Add a simple control (e.g. a toggle or checkbox) to switch to 'allow multiple open' mode.
In 'allow multiple open' mode, the user should be able to open more than one FAQ item at once.
expectedBehavior: Initially all FAQ items are closed.
Clicking a closed question opens its answer.
In single-open mode: opening one item automatically closes any other open item.
Switching to multi-open mode keeps already open items and allows opening others.
Clicking an open question closes its answer in both modes.
implementationNotes: Keep the data (questions/answers and open state) in the parent component. Holding `openIndexes` and `allowMultiple` in signals is the recommended form; replace the array on every change instead of pushing into it.

Create a child component (e.g. `FaqItemComponent`) that receives `question`, `answer`, and `isOpen` as inputs and emits a `toggle` event when its header is clicked. The solution declares them with `input.required()`, `input()` and `output()`; the starter's `@Input()`/`@Output()` fields work as well.
Use `@for` in the parent template to render FAQ items.
You can use simple CSS transitions (e.g. `max-height` or `opacity`) for a smooth open/close animation, but this is optional.
techFocus: Parent → child data flow with signal inputs and an output (`input()`, `output()`)
Controlled vs uncontrolled state (parent controlling which index is open)
Conditional rendering with `@if` and class binding (`[class.open]`)
Basic UI state toggling and list rendering

solutionBlock.overview:
This exercise is about lifting state up to the parent component and controlling which FAQ items are open. `AppComponent` holds the questions and answers in a constant `faqItems` array, the mode in `allowMultiple = signal(false)` and the open items in `openIndexes = signal<number[]>([])`. Each `FaqItemComponent` receives `question`, `answer` and `isOpen` as signal inputs, shows its answer only while `isOpen()` is true, and emits `toggle` when its header is clicked; it never decides on its own whether it is open.

In the default (single-open) mode, the parent keeps at most one index in `openIndexes`: a click either makes that index the only open one or clears it. In multi-open mode, the parent treats the array like a set and adds or removes the clicked index.

**Test cases**
- Initially, all answers are hidden.
- Click the first question → its answer becomes visible, others stay closed.
- In single-open mode, clicking a second question closes the first and opens the second.
- Switch to multi-open mode → currently open item(s) stay open, and you can open additional ones without closing the others.
- Clicking an open item closes it in both modes.

approaches.title: Open indexes in a parent signal, items as signal-input children
approaches.prose:
Split the work between a parent that owns every piece of state and a child that only renders.

1. `FaqItemComponent` declares `question = input.required<string>()`, `answer = input.required<string>()`, `isOpen = input(false)` and `toggle = output<void>()`. Its template reads `question()`, `answer()` and `isOpen()`, renders the answer inside `@if (isOpen())`, and `onHeaderClick()` calls `toggle.emit()`.
2. `AppComponent` keeps `faqItems` as a readonly array; the content never changes, so it needs no signal. The mode lives in `allowMultiple = signal(false)` and the open items in `openIndexes = signal<number[]>([])`.
3. `isItemOpen(index)` returns `openIndexes().includes(index)`, and the template calls it in `[isOpen]="isItemOpen(i)"`.
4. `onItemToggle(index)` checks the mode. In multi-open mode it calls `openIndexes.update(...)` with `filter` to close the item or a spread to open it; in single-open mode it calls `openIndexes.set(currentlyOpen ? [] : [index])`.
5. `onToggleAllowMultiple()` flips the mode with `update`. Switching back to single-open mode with several items open keeps only `indexes[0]`, the item opened first.

Every write hands the signal a new array. A `push` into the current array would not notify it: the items would still update here, because each change follows a click that marks the views for checking, but a `computed` over `openIndexes`, such as a count of open items, would keep its old value. With both components on `OnPush`, the child re-renders when its `isOpen` input changes and the parent when `openIndexes` or `allowMultiple` does.

pitfalls: Letting each item manage its own open/closed state, which makes it hard to enforce 'only one open at a time'.
Using index-based state but forgetting to clear other indexes in single-open mode.
Directly mutating the `faqItems` array to store UI-only state instead of keeping a separate `openIndexes` representation.
Pushing into or splicing the array held by `openIndexes`: the signal keeps the same reference and does not notify, so a `computed` over it keeps its old value.
Writing `@if (isOpen)` without the call in the child template: the input signal is a function, which is always truthy, so every answer shows.
techniques: Keeping view data (question/answer) separate from UI state (open indexes).
Declaring the child's API with `input.required()`, `input()` and `output()`, so the parent stays in full control of state.
Deriving `isItemOpen` from an array of indexes instead of storing booleans on each item.
Replacing the `openIndexes` array through `set` and `update` on every change.

description.summary: Build a simple paginated data table in Angular that shows a static list of users. Display 5 rows per page, with Previous / Next controls and a "Page X of Y" indicator. Disable the navigation buttons appropriately on the first and last pages. Concepts: components, state, pagination. Angular focus: keep page index in component state and derive page slices.

requirements: Use a standalone Angular component as the root component.
Render a static list (20–30 items) of users in a table (id, name, email, role).
Show 5 rows per page.
Add "Previous" and "Next" buttons to change the current page.
Display the current page and total pages (e.g. "Page 2 of 5").
Disable the "Previous" button on the first page.
Disable the "Next" button on the last page.
expectedBehavior: Initially, the table shows the first 5 users (page 1).
Clicking "Next" advances to the next 5 users, until the last page.
Clicking "Previous" goes back one page, until the first page.
On the first page, "Previous" is disabled and cannot change the page.
On the last page, "Next" is disabled and cannot change the page.
The label "Page X of Y" always reflects the state correctly (X is 1-based).
implementationNotes: Hold the 0-based page index in a signal (`currentPage = signal(0)`) and change it with `update`; the template reads it as `currentPage()`. The starter's plain `currentPage = 0` field also works here, because every change comes from a click in this template.
Keep the full list in a single readonly array on the component.
Derive `pagedUsers` with `computed`, slicing `pageSize` users starting at `currentPage() * pageSize`.
Derive `totalPages`, `isFirstPage` and `isLastPage` with `computed` as well, and bind the two flags to the buttons' `[disabled]`.
techFocus: Signal state for the page index (`currentPage`).
Handling edge cases in UI state (first/last page).
Clean template bindings for lists (`@for`) and button states (`[disabled]`).

solutionBlock.overview:
The table needs one piece of state: the index of the current page. The solution keeps it in a signal, `currentPage = signal(0)`, 0-based so it feeds the slice math directly. The 20 users come from `USERS` in `users.data.ts` and never change. Everything else is computed from those two: `totalPages`, the `pagedUsers` slice that fills the table body, and the `isFirstPage` and `isLastPage` flags that disable Previous and Next. The template reads them with call syntax, `@for (user of pagedUsers(); track user.id)` and `[disabled]="isFirstPage()"`, and renders the label as `Page {{ currentPage() + 1 }} of {{ totalPages() }}`.

**Test cases**
- Initial render → shows the first 5 users, the label reads `Page 1 of 4`, and Previous is disabled.
- Clicking Next repeatedly moves through the list in chunks of 5 until the last page, then Next becomes disabled.
- Clicking Previous from any page > 1 moves back a page until page 1.
- The label always matches the current page index, and buttons are never enabled when they should be disabled.

approaches.title: Signal page index with computed slice and flags
approaches.prose:
Keep the pagination in `AppComponent`. `users` points at the static `USERS` array and `pageSize` is 5; neither changes, so both stay plain readonly fields. The only state is the page index, `currentPage = signal(0)`.

Each derived value is a `computed`:
1. `totalPages` is `Math.ceil(this.users.length / this.pageSize) || 1`. The `|| 1` keeps one page, the label `Page 1 of 1` and both buttons disabled if the list is ever empty.
2. `pagedUsers` slices `users` from `start = currentPage() * pageSize` to `start + pageSize`. `slice` returns a new array and leaves `USERS` as it is.
3. `isFirstPage` compares `currentPage()` with 0, and `isLastPage` compares it with `totalPages() - 1`.

`goToPrevious()` and `goToNext()` check the matching flag before calling `currentPage.update(...)`, so the index stays inside the page range even when a caller ignores the disabled buttons.

A getter runs every time Angular checks the template; a `computed` keeps its result until a signal it read changes, so the slice is recalculated once per page change. `totalPages` reads no signal and is calculated once. It stays a `computed` so the template needs no change if `users` later becomes a signal fed by a filter or a request. Every value the template reads is a signal or a constant, which makes `OnPush` safe here.

pitfalls: Treating `currentPage` as 1-based while doing slice calculations, which makes `start` / `end` off by one.
Leaving `goToPrevious()` and `goToNext()` unguarded, so `currentPage` can go negative or past the last page.
Writing `pagedUsers` or `currentPage` in the template without the call parentheses: `@for` and the label then receive the signal function instead of its value.
Repeating the slice math inline in the template instead of one `computed`, which spreads the page arithmetic across bindings and reruns it on every check.
Not binding the buttons' disabled state, so users can still click Previous on the first page or Next on the last page.
techniques: Holding the page index in a `signal` and changing it with `update`.
Deriving the page count, the page slice and the first/last flags with `computed` instead of getters.
Slicing a static array for the view without mutating it.
Using `OnPush` change detection with a template that reads only signals and constants.

description.summary: Implement an Angular light/dark theme toggle with persistence. Store the theme in localStorage, apply it to the root element, and keep the toggle label/icon in sync across reloads and new sessions. Concepts: components, services, dependency-injection. Angular focus: use a ThemeService to persist theme and apply it to the root element.

requirements: Render a main page layout with a simple content card and a theme toggle control in the top-right corner.
Support two themes: "light" and "dark".
Store the current theme in a dedicated Angular service (global-ish state).
Persist the selected theme in localStorage under a stable key.
On initial load, read the theme from localStorage and apply it before the user interacts.
Apply the theme at the document level by setting `data-theme` on `<html>`, so that the existing CSS can react to it.

Edit the TypeScript files `/src/app/theme.service.ts` and `/src/app/app.component.ts`; in the template only the two `isDark` bindings change, and only if `isDark` becomes a `computed` (`isDark()`). All CSS files are already wired to respond to `data-theme` and should be left as-is.
expectedBehavior: By default, the app starts in light mode if there is no previous theme stored.
If the user toggles to dark mode, the page background, text, and card colors change.
Reloading the page keeps the user’s last theme selection (light or dark).
The toggle UI (label or icon) always reflects the actual current theme.
Switching themes is instant and does not require a full reload.
implementationNotes: `/src/app/theme.service.ts`: Use an Angular service (e.g. `ThemeService`) to hold global theme state in a signal, expose it read-only (`currentTheme = this.theme.asReadonly()`), read/write localStorage, and update the `data-theme` attribute on `<html>`.
`/src/app/app.component.ts`: Inject the service, derive `isDark` with `computed(() => this.themeService.currentTheme() === 'dark')`, and wire the toggle button to `themeService.toggleTheme()`.

The CSS in `/src/app/app.component.css` and `/src/styles.css` is already configured: it uses `:root` / `:root[data-theme='dark']` and `:host-context([data-theme='dark'])` rules to switch page, card, and toggle colors when `data-theme` changes.
You do not need to modify any CSS for this exercise; drive the theme state and `data-theme` from the service.
Wrap localStorage reads and writes in `try`/`catch`: storage access can throw, for example when the browser blocks site data, and the toggle should keep working for the session.
Avoid duplicating theme logic in multiple components; treat the service as the single source of truth.
techFocus: Global-ish state via a shared service that exposes a read-only signal
Deriving component state from a service signal with `computed`
Side-effects and initialization logic (constructor / app bootstrap)
Using localStorage safely in a browser environment
Simple theming by driving `data-theme` on `<html>` and letting existing CSS respond

solutionBlock.overview:
This exercise lifts theme state into a global Angular service and wires it to both the UI and the DOM. `ThemeService` keeps the current theme ("light" or "dark") in a private signal, reads the initial value from localStorage when it is created, and applies it to the `<html>` element through a `data-theme` attribute. It exposes the theme as a read-only signal, `currentTheme`, plus `setTheme()` and `toggleTheme()`. The root `AppComponent` injects the service, derives `isDark` from `currentTheme()` with `computed`, and hands every click to `toggleTheme()`. The provided CSS (in `styles.css` and `app.component.css`) already listens to `data-theme` using `:root[data-theme='dark']` and `:host-context([data-theme='dark'])`, so the styles stay as they are.

**Test cases**
- First visit with empty localStorage → app starts in light mode and shows the light theme.
- Click the toggle once → app switches to dark mode, the page background becomes dark, and the toggle shows dark mode.
- Reload the page after switching to dark mode → app initializes in dark mode, without a visible flash back to light.
- Toggle back to light → theme changes immediately and localStorage is updated.
- The toggle label/icon always matches the active theme. Key concepts: components, services, dependency-injection.

approaches.title: Global ThemeService with a theme signal and `data-theme` on `<html>`
approaches.prose:
Use a dedicated `ThemeService` as the global source of truth for the theme.

1. Define a `Theme` type alias (`'light' | 'dark'`) and a stable localStorage key, `uf-theme`.
2. Read storage through `safeReadTheme()` and write it through `safeWriteTheme()`. Both wrap `localStorage` in `try`/`catch`, because storage access throws in sandboxed frames and when site data is blocked. `safeWriteTheme()` also keeps the last choice in a module variable, `memoryTheme`, which the service falls back to when storage cannot be read.
3. Hold the theme in `theme = signal<Theme>(safeReadTheme() ?? memoryTheme)` and expose `currentTheme = this.theme.asReadonly()`, so components can read the theme but only the service changes it. The constructor applies it to `document.documentElement` with `setAttribute('data-theme', theme)`; the document comes from `inject(DOCUMENT)`.
4. `setTheme(theme)` sets the signal, writes storage and updates `data-theme`; `toggleTheme()` flips between `'light'` and `'dark'` through `setTheme`.
5. In `AppComponent`, inject the service and derive `isDark = computed(() => this.themeService.currentTheme() === 'dark')`. The template reads `isDark()` for the icon and the label, and the button calls `onToggleClick()`, which delegates to `toggleTheme()`.

The component never stores the theme itself. `isDark` recomputes from the service's signal, so a `setTheme()` call from any other component updates this toggle too, and `OnPush` is safe because the template reads nothing but that signal. The service is created when the root component first injects it, so a stored dark theme is on `<html>` before the component's first render.

pitfalls: Reading from localStorage too late (e.g. after the first render), causing a visible flash from light to dark.
Forgetting to actually apply the theme to the document (only changing the label but not colors).
Using multiple sources of truth for the theme (e.g. duplicating theme state in both component and service).
Keeping the theme in a plain service field while the component uses `OnPush`: a `setTheme()` call from another component does not mark this view, so the label goes stale.
Turning `isDark` into a `computed` but leaving `{{ isDark ? 'Dark' : 'Light' }}` in the template: the signal function itself is truthy, so the label always reads "Dark".
Trying to change the CSS instead of driving the existing `data-theme`-based styles from the service.
techniques: Using an Angular service as a global singleton that holds app-wide state in a signal and exposes it with `asReadonly()`.
Deriving `isDark` from the service signal with `computed`.
Injecting `DOCUMENT` with `inject()` to update the root element.
Encapsulating side-effects (localStorage reads/writes, DOM attribute updates) inside the service instead of scattering them across components.
Letting preconfigured CSS (`:root[data-theme='dark']` and `:host-context([data-theme='dark'])`) handle visual changes while the service only controls `data-theme`.

description.summary: Build a 3-step signup flow using Angular reactive forms: basic info, address info, and a summary plus submit step. Each step should only allow moving forward when its fields are valid.

requirements: Use a standalone Angular component as the root component.
Use Angular reactive forms (`FormGroup`, `FormBuilder`, `Validators`) with nested form groups.
Step 1 (Basic info): capture `name` and `email` fields.
Step 2 (Address info): capture `street`, `city`, `country`, and optionally `postalCode`.
Step 3 (Summary): display a read-only summary of all collected values and provide a `Submit` button.
The `Next` button should be disabled unless the current step's group is valid.
Preserve entered values when navigating back and forth between steps.
(Optional) Add a `Back` button to move to the previous step.
expectedBehavior: The flow starts on Step 1 (Basic info).
On Step 1, `Next` is disabled until both `name` and `email` are valid (required + valid email).
On Step 2, `Next` is disabled until required address fields are valid.
Clicking `Next` on a valid step moves to the next step.
Clicking `Back` moves to the previous step without losing already entered values.
On Step 3, the user sees a summary of all fields and a `Submit` button.
Clicking `Submit` validates the entire form and (for this exercise) logs or otherwise handles the collected data.
implementationNotes: Use a single top-level `FormGroup` with nested groups like `basic` and `address` to keep form state centralized.
Track the current step with a number index (0, 1, 2). Holding it in a signal (`currentStep = signal(0)`) lets `computed` flags and an `OnPush` view follow every step change.
Expose `basicGroup` and `addressGroup` for shorter template bindings. The nested groups never change, so readonly fields (`this.form.controls.basic`) are enough.
Use `markAllAsTouched()` before moving forward or submitting, so validation errors show up immediately.

Derive `isFirstStep`, `isLastStep`, and `canGoNext` with `computed` instead of scattering conditions in the template. A group's validity is not a signal: bridge it with `toSignal(group.statusChanges...)`, because a `computed` that reads `basicGroup.valid` directly re-runs only when `currentStep` changes.
techFocus: Step state in a signal, with `computed` navigation flags
Bridging form status into signals with `toSignal`
Basic UI architecture for a wizard-like flow

solutionBlock.overview:
This exercise keeps the whole signup in one reactive `FormGroup` and puts a stepper on top of it. `form` holds two nested groups, `basic` (`name`, `email`) and `address` (`street`, `city`, `country`, optional `postalCode`), and a `currentStep` signal (0, 1 or 2) picks the section that `@switch` renders.

The core idea is:
- Model all fields in one `FormGroup`, so the values survive while the step markup is swapped and `submit()` reads a single payload.
- Gate `Next` on the current group only: `canGoNext` is a `computed` over `currentStep` and the validity of `basic` or `address`.
- Derive `isFirstStep` and `isLastStep` with `computed` instead of repeating the comparisons in the template.

**Test cases**
- Initial load → Step 1 is shown, `Next` is disabled.
- Fill valid `name` and `email`, click `Next` → moves to Step 2.
- On Step 2 with invalid address fields → `Next` stays disabled and/or shows validation errors when attempted.
- After filling valid address, click `Next` → Step 3 shows a summary of all values.
- Click `Back` from Step 3 → Step 2 is shown with previously entered data intact.
- Click `Submit` on Step 3 with valid data → form is processed (e.g. logged) and no validation errors are shown.

approaches.title: One FormGroup with nested groups and a step signal
approaches.prose:
Build `form` with `inject(FormBuilder)` as a class field: a `basic` group with a required `name` and an `email` checked by `Validators.required` and `Validators.email`, and an `address` group with required `street`, `city` and `country` plus an optional `postalCode`. `basicGroup` and `addressGroup` are plain fields pointing at `form.controls.basic` and `form.controls.address`; the template reads the error flags and the summary values through them.

The step lives in `currentStep = signal(0)`, and `isFirstStep` and `isLastStep` are computed from it. `canGoNext` also needs the current group's validity, which is not a signal: a `computed` that read `basicGroup.valid` would re-run only when the step changes and leave `Next` disabled while the user types. `basicValid` and `addressValid` therefore bridge each group's `statusChanges` with `toSignal`, starting from the group's current `valid`, and `canGoNext` returns the one that matches `currentStep()`.

`next()` marks the current group as touched, returns while it is invalid, and otherwise advances with `currentStep.update((step) => step + 1)`; `prev()` steps back unless the first step is showing. `submit()` marks the whole form as touched, returns if it is invalid, logs `form.value` and sets `submitMessage`, which `next()` and `prev()` clear. The inline errors read `touched` and `invalid` straight from the controls. Those change on blur, typing and button clicks, which are template events, so the `OnPush` view is already marked for check.

pitfalls: Managing each step as a completely separate form, which makes it harder to submit a single payload at the end.
Allowing `Next` to move forward even when the current step is invalid, causing confusing validation behavior on later steps.
Not marking controls as touched before checking validity, so users never see why they cannot proceed.
Deriving `canGoNext` with a `computed` that reads `basicGroup.valid` directly: form validity is not a signal, so the button only updates when `currentStep` changes.
Setting `currentStep` from the template instead of in `next()` and `prev()`, which skips the per-step validity check.
techniques: Grouping related fields under nested `FormGroup`s (`basic`, `address`) for cleaner validation and payload structure.
Keeping the step in a signal and deriving `isFirstStep`, `isLastStep` and `canGoNext` with `computed`.
Turning a group's `statusChanges` into a signal with `toSignal`, so a `computed` can depend on its validity.
Calling `markAllAsTouched()` before moving forward or submitting to surface validation errors.
Using `@switch (currentStep())` in the template so each step's markup sits in its own block.

description.summary: Build a small shopping cart UI using an Angular standalone component. Render a product list with "Add to cart" buttons and a cart section where you can increase/decrease quantities, remove items, and show derived totals. Concepts: components, state, derived-state.

requirements: Use a standalone Angular component as the root component.
Render a static product list with name and price for each product.
Each product should have an "Add to cart" button.
Render a cart section that lists all items currently in the cart.
Each cart item should show name, unit price, quantity, and line total (price × quantity).
In the cart, allow increasing and decreasing the quantity of an item.
Allow removing an item from the cart entirely.
Show derived totals: overall item count (total quantity) and total price for the entire cart.
Keep the cart state in a nested structure (e.g. an array of `cartItems`).
expectedBehavior: Clicking "Add to cart" for a product adds it to the cart with quantity 1 (or increments the quantity if it already exists).
Clicking "+" in the cart increases that item's quantity by 1.
Clicking "−" in the cart decreases that item's quantity by 1; if it reaches 0, the item can be removed or clamped at 1 (depending on your chosen UX).
Clicking "Remove" deletes the item from the cart.
Total quantity updates whenever items are added, removed, or their quantities change.
Total price updates whenever items are added, removed, or their quantities change.
UI stays in sync with state without manual DOM manipulation.
implementationNotes: Use a nested state structure for the cart, e.g. `cartItems: { id, name, price, quantity }[]`.

Hold the cart in a signal (`cartItems = signal<CartItem[]>([])`) and change it only with immutable updates (`map`, `filter`, spread). A signal compares by reference, so `push` or `item.quantity++` on the current array does not notify it.
Derive `totalQty` and `totalPrice` with `computed` instead of storing totals separately; the starter's getters mark where they go.
Keep the state and update methods on the component; you do not need NgRx or a global store for this exercise.
Use `@for` with stable product and cart-item ids for rendering lists of products and cart items.
techFocus: Signal state for nested cart items
Derived state with `computed` (total quantity, total price)
Template bindings for lists and events

solutionBlock.overview:
The cart is an array of lines, each a product plus a `quantity`, held in one signal: `cartItems = signal<CartItem[]>([])`. `totalQty` and `totalPrice` are computed from it with `reduce`, so the header totals cannot drift from the lines. Every method replaces the array: `addToCart` appends a new line or raises the quantity of an existing one, `increaseQty` and `decreaseQty` swap in a copy of one line with the quantity changed, and `removeItem` filters a line out. "−" on a line with quantity 1 removes it. The products come from the constant `PRODUCTS` array and are listed above the cart.

**Test cases**
- Clicking "Add to cart" adds a line with quantity 1; clicking it again for the same product raises that line to 2 instead of adding a second line.
- "+" and "−" change one line's quantity by 1 and update its line total, the total items count and the total price.
- "−" on a line with quantity 1 removes the line.
- "Remove" deletes the line whatever its quantity.
- Removing the last line shows the empty cart message, and the header reads `Total items: 0 · Total: $0.00`.

approaches.title: Cart signal with immutable updates and computed totals
approaches.prose:
`PRODUCTS` never changes, so `products` stays a plain readonly field. The cart is `cartItems = signal<CartItem[]>([])`, where `CartItem` extends `Product` with a `quantity`.

1. `totalQty` and `totalPrice` are `computed` values that `reduce` over `cartItems()`. They recalculate when the signal receives a new array, and no total is stored separately.
2. `addToCart(product)` checks `cartItems()` for a line with the same `id`. If one exists, it calls `changeQuantity(product.id, 1)`; otherwise it appends `{ ...product, quantity: 1 }` through `update`.
3. `changeQuantity(id, delta)` maps over the lines and replaces only the matching one with `{ ...line, quantity: line.quantity + delta }`. `increaseQty` passes 1. `decreaseQty` passes -1, or calls `removeItem` when the line is already at 1, so no line ever shows a quantity of 0.
4. `removeItem(item)` filters the line out by `id`.

Each change gives the signal a new array, and a changed line is a new object. A signal compares with `Object.is`, so `push` or `item.quantity++` on the current array would not notify it, and `totalQty` and `totalPrice` would keep showing their cached results. The template calls `totalQty()`, `totalPrice()` and `cartItems()`, formats prices with `CurrencyPipe` (imported on its own instead of `CommonModule`) and tracks lines by `item.id`. With every changing value in a signal, the component uses `OnPush`.

pitfalls: Mutating the existing `cartItems` array (`push`, `splice`) or a line's `quantity` in place: the signal keeps the same reference, so the computed totals stop following the lines.
Duplicating products in the cart instead of merging them and increasing `quantity`.
Trying to manually keep track of `totalPrice` and `totalQty` as separate state instead of deriving them from `cartItems`, which can easily drift out of sync.
Not handling the edge case when decreasing quantity to zero (e.g. leaving zero-quantity items in the cart).
techniques: Holding the cart in a `signal` and changing it with `update`, using spread (`[...]`), `map` and `filter`.
Using TypeScript interfaces to model products and cart items.
Deriving `totalQty` and `totalPrice` with `computed` to keep state single-sourced.
Importing `CurrencyPipe` on its own instead of `CommonModule`.
Using `@for` with stable ids to render and update lists efficiently.

description.summary: Implement an Angular debounced search using RxJS. Use debounceTime + distinctUntilChanged + switchMap to cancel stale requests, and model loading, error, and empty states so the UI feels like a real search box. This checks reactive streams, cancellation, and UI state coordination. Angular focus: debounce with RxJS debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged, and switchMap cancellation.

requirements: Use a standalone Angular component as the root component.
Render a search input where the user can type a query.
Do NOT call the fake API on every keystroke; debounce input so the search runs 500ms after the user stops typing.
Perform a fake async search call (e.g. in-memory array) that returns results based on the query text.
Show a loading state while the debounced search request is in flight.
Show an error state when the fake API fails.
Show a list of matching results when the request succeeds.
When the query is cleared, cancel the pending search and clear the results.
expectedBehavior: Typing quickly in the input does not trigger multiple API calls; only the final value after the user pauses for 500ms is searched.
While a search is running, a small loading label (e.g. "Searching…") is visible.
If the fake API throws an error, an error message is displayed and loading is cleared.
On success, results are rendered as a list. Updating the query triggers a new debounced search.
Clearing the query clears both the loading state and the results list.
Subscriptions are cleaned up when the component is destroyed (no memory leaks).
implementationNotes: Use RxJS to handle debouncing and cancellation.
A common pattern is a `Subject<string>` for search terms, piped through `debounceTime(500)` and `distinctUntilChanged()`.
Use `switchMap` so that a newer term cancels the request still in flight for an older one once the newer term has passed the debounce.
Use `tap` to toggle `isLoading` and reset error state before each search.
Use `catchError` to handle errors from the fake API and surface them as UI state.

Keep `query`, `results`, `isLoading` and `error` in signals. The pipeline writes the last three from timer callbacks after the input event has been handled, and under `OnPush` only signal writes refresh the view from there.
End the subscription with `takeUntilDestroyed(destroyRef)`; it replaces a `destroy$` subject completed in `ngOnDestroy`.
You can simulate a fake API with an in-memory array and `of(...).pipe(delay(...))`. You may also deliberately throw for specific queries (e.g. "error") to test the error state.
techFocus: Loading, error and result state in signals

solutionBlock.overview:
Use a standalone Angular component with a `Subject<string>` for search terms. `onQueryChange()` sets the `query` signal and pushes the raw value into `searchTerm$`. The pipeline runs `debounceTime(500)` and `distinctUntilChanged()`, so a burst of typing becomes one search, then `switchMap`s into `fakeApiSearch()`, which answers after 600ms from an in-memory list and fails on purpose for the query `error`.

`results`, `isLoading` and `error` are signals that the pipeline writes: `tap` sets the loading flag (or clears the results for an empty query) and resets the error, `catchError` records the error message, and the subscriber stores the results. `takeUntilDestroyed` ends the subscription with the component.

**Key ideas**
- Represent user input as a stream (`Subject<string>`).
- Use `debounceTime` + `distinctUntilChanged` + `switchMap` to control when and how the fake API runs.
- Keep `results`, `isLoading`, and `error` in signals that the pipeline writes, so the `OnPush` view follows each stage of the search.

approaches.title: Subject-based stream with debounce, switchMap and signal state
approaches.prose:
`onQueryChange(value)` runs on every `input` event. It sets `query` at once, so the status line names the new text, and pushes the value into `searchTerm$`. `setupSearchStream()`, called from the constructor, pipes that subject through `debounceTime(500)` and `distinctUntilChanged()`: rapid typing collapses into one value, and a value equal to the last searched term is dropped.

A `tap` then prepares the state. An empty or whitespace-only term clears `results` and `isLoading`; any other term sets `isLoading` to `true`; both reset `error`. `switchMap` returns `of([])` for an empty term and otherwise calls `fakeApiSearch(trimmed)`. When a newer term clears the debounce, `switchMap` unsubscribes from the older request, so its response never lands. `catchError` stores the error message, clears `isLoading` and recovers with an empty list, and the subscriber writes `results` and clears `isLoading`.

`results`, `isLoading` and `error` are signals because the pipeline writes them from timer callbacks, after the input event has been handled. Under `OnPush`, plain fields set there would not reach the screen until the next keystroke. `query` is a signal as well, so everything the template reads comes from one. `takeUntilDestroyed(this.destroyRef)` ends the subscription when the component is destroyed, which replaces the `destroy$` subject and `ngOnDestroy`.

pitfalls: Calling the fake API directly from the input handler without debounce, which causes unnecessary requests.
Using `mergeMap` instead of `switchMap`, so old requests can overwrite newer results.
Forgetting to clear `isLoading` on error, leaving the UI stuck in a loading state.
Not handling the empty-query case (should clear results and avoid calling the API).
Writing plain fields from the pipeline in an `OnPush` component: the callbacks run on timers after the input event, so the view keeps showing the state from the last keystroke.
Leaking subscriptions by never unsubscribing when the component is destroyed.
techniques: Subject + RxJS operators for debounced UI events.
Cancellable async work with `switchMap`.
Error handling with `catchError` and safe fallbacks.
Signals for the state that RxJS callbacks write and the `OnPush` template reads.
Subscription cleanup with `takeUntilDestroyed` and an injected `DestroyRef`.

description.summary: Implement a reusable star-rating widget as an Angular standalone component. It should render a row of clickable stars, allow the user to select a rating with the mouse or the arrow keys, and notify the parent when the rating changes. Concepts: components, inputs-outputs, event-binding. Angular focus: a controlled rating component that the parent binds with `[(rating)]`, written with `input()` and `model()`.

requirements: Create a standalone `StarRatingComponent` that renders a row of stars.
Support a configurable maximum number of stars through a `max` input (default 5).
Accept the current rating as a `rating` input so the parent controls the value.
Emit `ratingChange` with the new value when the user selects a rating, so the parent can bind `[(rating)]`.
Make the stars a radio group: `role="radio"` and `aria-checked` on each star, one Tab stop for the whole group, and the arrow keys to change the rating.
Use the widget from a simple `AppComponent` and show the current rating below it.
expectedBehavior: Stars render from 1 up to the configured `max` (e.g. 5).
Clicking a star sets the rating to that star index (e.g. clicking the 4th star sets rating to 4).
All stars with index less than or equal to the rating appear visually "filled".
The parent component sees the updated rating value (e.g. via `[(rating)]` or an output event).
With a star focused, Right or Down checks the next star and moves focus to it, and Left or Up the previous one; from the last star Right goes to the first, and from the first Left goes to the last.
Tab reaches the rating once, on the checked star, or on the first star before anything is rated.
implementationNotes: Use `@for` in the star-rating template to loop over an array of star indices.

The recommended form is `max = input(5)` and `rating = model(0)`: a model is an input the child can also set, and setting it emits `ratingChange`. The starter's `@Input()` fields with an `@Output()` emitter work as well when `onRate` assigns the rating and emits it.
Use class binding (`[class.filled]`) to fill every star up to the current rating.
Derive the star values (`[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` for a `max` of 5) in one place: `computed` over `max()` with signals, or the starter's `stars` getter with plain fields.

Follow the WAI-ARIA rating radio group: `role="radiogroup"` with a label on the container, `role="radio"` and `aria-checked` on each star (true only for the selected one), `tabindex="0"` on the checked star or on the first star before any rating, and `tabindex="-1"` on the rest. `aria-pressed` would turn every filled star into a pressed toggle button.

Handle the arrow keys in a `keydown` listener on each star: call `preventDefault()` so the page does not scroll, set the rating, and move focus to the star you checked. `viewChildren` gives the component its star buttons.
techFocus: Signal inputs and `model()` for parent–child two-way binding
A keyboard-operable radio group with a roving tabindex

solutionBlock.overview:
This exercise builds a reusable star rating control whose value belongs to the parent. `StarRatingComponent` reads its scale from a signal input, `max = input(5)`, and its value from a model, `rating = model(0)`. A model is an input that the child can also write: `rating.set(value)` changes the value the child renders and emits `ratingChange`, the event that Angular's `[(rating)]` syntax listens to. `AppComponent` keeps the value in `currentRating = signal(0)` and binds `[(rating)]="currentRating"`, so a click on a star updates the parent's signal and the hint below the widget. The stars form a radio group: each is a `role="radio"` button whose `aria-checked` is true only for the selected star, one star at a time is in the Tab order, and the arrow keys move the rating the way they move any radio group.

**Test cases**
- Initial state: rating is `0` → no stars are filled.
- Click the 3rd star → rating becomes `3` and three stars appear filled.
- Click the 5th star → rating becomes `5` and five stars appear filled.
- Updating the rating from the parent (e.g. `currentRating.set(2)`) updates the visual state of the widget.
- When `max` is changed (e.g. to 10), the component renders that many stars.
- Focus the 2nd star and press Right → rating becomes `3` and focus moves to the 3rd star.
- Press Left on the 1st star → rating becomes `5` and focus moves to the 5th star.
- Before any rating, only the 1st star has `tabindex="0"`; after a rating, only the checked star has it.

approaches.title: Child component with a signal input and a `rating` model
approaches.prose:
Keep the stars in `StarRatingComponent` and the value in `AppComponent`.

1. Declare `max = input(5)` and `rating = model(0)` in the child. Its template reads them as `max()` and `rating()`.
2. Derive `stars = computed(() => Array.from({ length: this.max() }, (_, i) => i + 1))`. The `[1, 2, …, max]` array is rebuilt only when `max` changes, where a getter builds a new one on every change detection pass. The template loops with `@for (star of stars(); track star)`; each value is unique, so it also serves as the track key.
3. Each button is a `role="radio"` that binds `[class.filled]="star <= rating()"`, `[attr.aria-checked]="star === rating()"` and an `aria-label` such as "3 out of 5". Exactly one star is checked. `aria-pressed` would make every star a toggle button, so a rating of 3 would be read as three pressed buttons.
4. `onRate(star)` returns early for values outside `1..max`, then calls `rating.set(value)`. That one call updates the child and emits `ratingChange` with the new value, so the child declares no separate output.
5. `tabStop` is computed from the rating: the checked star, or the first star while the rating is 0. Each button binds `[attr.tabindex]="star === tabStop() ? 0 : -1"`, so Tab enters the group once and leaves it with the next press.
6. `onKeydown(event, star)` looks the key up in `ARROW_STEPS`, +1 for Right and Down and -1 for Left and Up, and ignores other keys. It calls `preventDefault()` so the page does not scroll, wraps past either end with `((star - 1 + step + count) % count) + 1`, sets the rating through `onRate`, and focuses the new star through `starButtons = viewChildren<ElementRef<HTMLButtonElement>>('starButton')`. Space and Enter need no handler: they click the focused button.
7. `AppComponent` holds `currentRating = signal(0)` and binds `[(rating)]="currentRating"`, passing the signal without parentheses. Angular reads it for the `rating` input and calls `currentRating.set(...)` when `ratingChange` fires. The hint shows `{{ currentRating() }}`.

Both components use `OnPush`. The child's bindings read `rating()` and `max()`, and the parent's hint reads `currentRating()`, so a change to any of them marks the view that reads it for checking. One difference from the `@Input()`/`@Output()` version: a model emits only when its value changes, so clicking the star that is already selected sends no `ratingChange`, while the `EventEmitter` version emitted the same value again.

pitfalls: Hardcoding five stars in the template instead of looping over `stars()`, which ignores `max`.
Writing `[(rating)]="currentRating()"`: a two-way binding has to write back, so it takes the signal itself, and Angular rejects the call with "Unsupported expression in a two-way binding".
Assigning `this.rating = value` out of habit from the decorator version: the field holds a model, so the value goes through `this.rating.set(value)`, which is also what emits `ratingChange`.
Keeping a second copy of the rating in the child: the model already is the child's value, and a copy goes stale when the parent sets a new rating.
Not visually differentiating filled vs empty stars, making the rating unclear.
Putting `aria-pressed` on every filled star: it describes toggle buttons, so a rating of 3 is announced as three pressed buttons instead of one checked choice.
Leaving every star in the Tab order: a radio group is one Tab stop, and the arrow keys move inside it.
techniques: Declaring a two-way bindable value with `model()`, which creates the `rating` input and the `ratingChange` output together.
Reading configuration through a signal input with a default, `max = input(5)`.
Deriving the star list with `computed` instead of a getter.
Binding a parent signal two-way with `[(rating)]="currentRating"`.
Building a focused, reusable standalone component that can be dropped into other views.
The WAI-ARIA radio group pattern: `role="radio"` with `aria-checked`, a roving `tabindex`, and arrow keys that wrap at the ends.
Focusing the newly checked star through a `viewChildren` signal query.
